Timeline::TimelineIndexAccessor::rolling_count¶

Back to Timeline Index Accessor API Reference

Signature¶

pluss::Series Timeline::TimelineIndexAccessor::rolling_count(const Duration& window) const

What It Does¶

Counts how many observations fall inside each trailing time window.

Unlike fixed-row rolling windows, this is time-aware: the membership of a window depends on the timestamp spacing, not just on row count.

That makes it useful on irregular clocks where “last 45 minutes” and “last 3 rows” are not even close to the same question.

Parameters¶

window

The trailing duration window. Examples include:

  • pluss::duration::minutes(15)

  • pluss::duration::minutes(45)

  • pluss::duration::hours(2)

In the current implementation the window is trailing and inclusive of values whose timestamp is still at least current_timestamp - window.

Returns¶

pluss::Series A 1D numeric Series with one rolling count per original observation.

Examples¶

Example 1. Count how many observations fall inside a trailing 45-minute window.

auto counts = idx.rolling_count(pluss::duration::minutes(45));
std::cout << pluss::series::print(counts) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 2, 3, 3, 3]

Example 2. Increase the duration when you want each trailing window to see further backward in time.

auto counts = idx.rolling_count(pluss::duration::minutes(60));
std::cout << pluss::series::print(counts) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 2, 3, 4, 4]

Notes¶

  • This is the right primitive when you care about observation density through time, not row position.

  • Widening the window can only keep the count the same or increase it.

  • For rolling numeric aggregation on an aligned values vector, use rolling_sum.
